title: Hugh Lofting
summary:
This document is a biographical article about Hugh Lofting (1886–1947), the English-American writer and trained civil engineer best known for creating the classic children's character Doctor Dolittle. The document begins with an overview of his life, noting that the character originated in illustrated letters he wrote to his children from the trenches during World War I, after which he settled in the United States.

The **Personal life** section details his birth in Maidenhead, Berkshire, his English and Irish ancestry, his education at Mount St Mary's College and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, his travels as a civil engineer, and his enlistment in the Irish Guards during World War I. It describes how, unwilling to write to his children about the horrors of war, he instead sent imaginative letters that became the foundation for his Doctor Dolittle novels. It also covers his serious war wounds, emigration to Killingworth, Connecticut in 1919, his three marriages, three children, and his death in 1947 in Topanga, California from cirrhosis of the liver.

The **Doctor Dolittle** section describes the fictional physician who lives in Puddleby-on-the-Marsh and can speak to animals, with stories set in 1820s–1840s England. It lists the series' publications, noting that The Story of Doctor Dolittle (1920) began the series and that its sequel, The Voyages of Doctor Dolittle (1922), won a Newbery Medal.

The **Other works for children** section covers his non-Dolittle books, including The Story of Mrs Tubbs and Tommy, Tilly, and Mrs. Tubbs (picture books), Porridge Poetry (his only non-Dolittle work still in print), Noisy Nora (a cautionary tale), and The Twilight of Magic (for older readers, notably the only book illustrated by someone else, Lois Lenski).

The **Victory for the Slain** section discusses his only work for adults, a 1942 anti-war poem in seven parts, published only in the United Kingdom.

The document concludes with lists of his published books, references, and external links to his works available through various digital archives and websites.
